finding.title: AnyDesk can let someone control this computer
finding.description:
AnyDesk lets someone else see and control this computer. Added on 20 January 2026. We didn't find a part of it that starts by itself, so it most likely works only while it's open. It isn't running right now. It last let someone in on 2 February 2026 (3 times in its log).

Scammers who call or show a pop-up often ask people to install tools like this, then use it to get into bank accounts or take payments. If you installed it yourself and still use it, that's fine. If you don't remember how it got here, think back to around when it was added.

What to do: decide whether it's yours. If it is, you can mark it as yours. If it isn't, or someone who contacted you asked you to install it, follow the steps for this card.

markable.label: AnyDesk
shows: Lets someone in without a click
markable.will_change: The checkup will stop warning you about AnyDesk. It will still be listed, as "marked as yours", on every checkup and in anything you export, so anyone helping you can see it. If its connections or its unattended access changes, the warning comes back.
how_to_undo: Choose "Stop treating this as mine" on the item in this app
markable.tech_undo: rescue known remove <id> (rescue known list shows the id)

remediation.title: Check a remote-access tool (TeamViewer, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect and others)

steps.title: Decide whether it's yours
steps.body:
Think back to around the date the finding gives for when it was added.

1. Did you install it yourself, or did a shop or IT person you contacted
   install it for you? If you still use it, it's yours: you can mark it as
   yours, and the checkup will stop warning about it until something changes,
   such as a new connection.
2. Did someone who contacted you (a call, a pop-up, an email or a text that
   said something was wrong with your computer, an account, a refund or a
   payment) ask you to install it? Treat it as a scam and follow Step 6.
3. If you don't remember, look at when it last let someone in, if the finding
   says. A connection you don't remember is a reason to remove it.

steps.title: Turn off unattended access
steps.body:
If the finding says it can let someone in without you clicking yes, it has a
part that starts by itself and waits for connections.

1. If you keep the tool, open its own settings and turn off unattended
   access (TeamViewer: "Grant easy access" and "Start TeamViewer with
   system"; AnyDesk: "Unattended access" under Security). Set a new
   password for it if it has one.
2. Check its list of trusted devices or contacts and remove any you don't
   recognise.

steps.title: Remove it if you don't need it
steps.body:
1. On a Mac: quit the tool, then drag it from Applications to the Trash.
   Some tools (AnyDesk, TeamViewer) also have an uninstall option in their
   own menu, which removes the part that starts by itself.
2. On Windows: open Settings, then Apps, then Installed apps, find the tool,
   and choose Uninstall.
3. Restart the computer and run the checkup again to make sure it's gone.

steps.title: Check for a second tool
steps.body:
Scammers often install a second remote-access tool, so that removing one
doesn't lock them out.

1. Run the checkup again after removing a tool.
2. If it finds another remote-access tool you didn't install, go back to
   Step 2 for that one too.

remediation.safety_note: Before you remove or turn anything off: if you think someone close to you set this up to watch you, removing it can alert them. Talk to an advocate first. In the US: National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788.
